html:
Slovak emigration to America was the mass departure of poor peasants from the Slovak counties of northern Hungary to the United States between about 1880 and 1914. Hundreds of thousands left, more than from almost any other region of Europe in proportion to its size.

Land was scarce, families large and wages low, and pressure to adopt Hungarian language added to the push. Most went to the coal mines and steel mills of Pennsylvania and Ohio. Their remittances kept villages alive. Slovak American groups backed national claims, and in 1918 Czech and Slovak exiles signed the Pittsburgh Agreement with Masaryk, promising Slovaks self rule in the new Czechoslovakia. The United States still has one of the largest Slovak communities abroad.
